task.goal: Design a neighborhood exchange of used household items that stays useful without becoming an unmonitored dumping site.
hard_constraints: Two volunteers have a covered public table for four Saturdays and no storage room.
No collection of participant names, money or hazardous electronics.
Track reuse, leftovers, cleanup time and exclusion of people who cannot lift heavy items.
task.available_resources: Printed item tags and a municipal disposal guide.
task.expected_result: A practical exchange flow with leftovers handled.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Small-item table with mandatory donor take-back
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is temporary display with donor responsibility: an item enters only while its donor remains present and agrees to remove anything unclaimed. This prevents the table from becoming a disposal service.

Run a short, clearly posted exchange window on each of four Saturdays, followed by a closing period with no admissions. One volunteer checks arrivals and tags items; the other supervises browsing, records outcomes and keeps the table orderly. Accept only clean, usable household items that fit safely on the table and can be handled comfortably by one person. Reject hazardous electronics, damaged goods and oversized loads. No money changes hands and no participant names are collected.

Each printed tag carries an item number, brief description and simple outcome boxes: taken, returned to donor, or abandoned. Donors stay within sight of their items; recipients take selected goods immediately. Stop intake whenever the table becomes crowded. At closing, donors collect leftovers. Give the municipal disposal guide to anyone whose item is rejected or remains unwanted; do not promise municipal collection.

Record items admitted, transfers observed, closing leftovers, abandoned items and cleanup minutes. Also tally heavy-item refusals and anonymous reports of being unable to carry an otherwise wanted item. Volunteers can offer reachable placement and light-item assistance without promising heavy lifting.

This needs only tags, the disposal guide, two volunteers and the table. It assumes donors will stay and comply with take-back. Deliberate abandonment remains possible; public-site authorization and an existing municipal route for any abandoned goods must be checked before launch. Without such a route, the exchange cannot guarantee a clean site.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: On the first Saturday, compare two equal, capacity-limited periods: ordinary supervised browsing and the same flow with the take-back rule explicitly explained at entry. Apply the rule throughout. Count completed transfers, donor departures leaving items behind, leftovers and cleanup minutes. The mechanism is weakened if explaining responsibility does not prevent abandonment or requires more supervision than two volunteers can provide. Treat this small comparison as operational evidence, not a reliable causal estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Live handoff exchange with no deposited inventory
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is eliminating unattended inventory. Donors keep possession of every item until a recipient accepts it; the public table functions as a staffed introduction point rather than a collection surface.

For each of four Saturdays, advertise one short, fixed meeting window. At arrival, a volunteer checks that an offered item is usable and excludes hazardous electronics. The donor receives an anonymous numbered tag describing the item and retains the item nearby without blocking access. Tags displayed on the table let browsers see offers without lifting or searching through piles. The second volunteer connects interested recipients with donors using item numbers. There is no payment, participant-name collection or exchange of contact details managed by the volunteers.

A transfer counts only when the recipient accepts and removes the item during the session. Unmatched donors leave with their belongings. At closing, remove all offer tags and inspect the table and immediate surrounding area. Provide the municipal disposal guide for unwanted goods. There is no overnight inventory or promise to receive items later.

Keep offers within a manageable nearby waiting area. Reject items that require unsafe lifting, obstruct access or cannot leave with their donor. Recipients may use their own companion for carrying, but the exchange provides no guaranteed transport or lifting service. Count offers, completed handoffs, unmatched offers, physically abandoned objects and cleanup minutes separately. Count offers refused for handling reasons and matches that fail because someone cannot lift or carry the item.

This assumes donors can wait and that the site permits a small gathering. Its principal limits are waiting time, weather outside the covered table and reduced participation by people who cannot transport goods. Two volunteers can operate it only if arrivals remain modest; pause admissions when either volunteer loses oversight.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the first Saturday, compare actual completed handoffs with anonymous tag selections: how many items would browsers choose, and how many leave successfully? Record waiting time approximately using session checkpoints. If many selections fail because donors cannot be located, waiting becomes excessive, or lifting prevents transfer, the tag-mediated handoff adds friction without delivering useful reuse. Inspect for abandoned objects immediately after closing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Request-first exchange with demand-gated arrivals
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is requiring evidence of demand before goods arrive. People first post anonymous requests; later Saturdays admit only items matching those requests. This reduces speculative donations and concentrates limited volunteer attention on potentially useful transfers.

On Saturday one, use printed tags to collect requests for specific, small household items. Each request states acceptable condition, approximate size and handling needs, with no participant name or contact information. Give it a number and let the requester retain a matching numbered tag. Display requests while staffed so prospective donors can note what to bring the following Saturday. Volunteers retain only the anonymous paper tags between sessions; no goods remain at the site.

On Saturdays two through four, display outstanding requests and check arriving offers against them. Requesters return during a clearly stated opening window with their numbered tags. Donors remain with matching items until handoff; if the requester does not appear or declines the item, the donor takes it home. Requests are invitations, not guaranteed reservations. Stop creating requests after Saturday three so the final session has no implied future service.

Reject hazardous electronics and unsafe, dirty or unmanageable goods. No money is collected. Request tags should explicitly allow people to specify a carryable weight or need for a companion. Do not promise lifting help. Count requests, matching offers, completed transfers, unmatched goods returned, abandoned items and cleanup minutes. Separately tally unmet handling needs, heavy-item refusals and transfers lost because of lifting difficulties. Give donors the municipal disposal guide for unwanted leftovers.

This needs tags, two volunteers and safe custody of a small paper bundle. It assumes enough residents return across Saturdays and donors consult the requests before bringing goods. It may miss spontaneous useful exchanges and works poorly with low repeat attendance. Custody rules and an existing municipal abandonment procedure remain necessary.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use Saturday one to tally both specific requests and unsolicited offers without accepting goods. On Saturday two, measure how many requested items arrive and complete a transfer. Compare their transfer proportion with the proportion of unsolicited offers that matched a recorded request on Saturday one. If demand-gating produces few completed transfers, frequent no-shows or substantial carrying exclusion, repeat attendance is too weak to justify this mechanism.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Accept only items with a verified same-day disposal exit
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is a guaranteed second exit: admit an item only if it can either be reused during the session or legally removed through an existing disposal route that afternoon. Donors may leave after acceptance. Intake is limited by the two volunteers’ ability to clear every admitted item themselves, even if nothing is taken.

Before the first Saturday, inspect the municipal disposal guide. Verify that an existing nearby public facility accepts relevant household materials, permits disposal by the volunteers, and is accessible after closing on all four Saturdays without payment or equipment. This is a prerequisite, not a promised municipal service. If no such route exists, this alternative is unavailable.

Post the accepted categories and session times using printed tags. Accept only clean, usable, non-electronic items that fit safely on the table and within the verified disposal rules. Exclude hazardous electronics and anything requiring heavy lifting. Start with a conservative total load that the volunteers can comfortably carry away in one trip without additional containers. Do not replenish that load allowance when items are claimed: this keeps cumulative intake bounded during the pilot.

One volunteer screens and tags arrivals; the other supervises selection and records departures. No names or money are collected. Recipients remove items immediately. Stop admissions before closing, count remaining goods, then clear them through the verified route. Nothing stays overnight.

Record admitted items, observed reuse, closing leftovers, actual disposal, abandoned goods outside intake, and cleanup minutes through completed clearance. Separately tally handling-related refusals and selections that fail because a recipient cannot carry the item. Keep goods within easy reach and offer assistance only within each volunteer’s safe ability.

This needs the table, tags, guide and a verified nearby exit. It trades broader participation and potentially reusable leftovers for predictable clearance. Unauthorized dumping nearby remains possible and must follow the site’s existing reporting procedure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before opening, walk the proposed clearance route and verify its rules and Saturday availability. On Saturday one, admit a very small batch and measure completed reuse, leftovers, carrying exclusions and full clearance time. Compare the required cleanup with a timed empty-table closing inspection, the simplest baseline. Failure to clear every accepted leftover legally in one safe trip falsifies the operating assumption; do not repeat deposited intake until that failure is resolved. This checks feasibility, not whether disposal-backed intake improves reuse relative to donor take-back.

EXPAND.title: Build complete household kits from complementary items
EXPAND.proposal:
The main mechanism is complementarity: combine individually unwanted items into a complete, useful kit. A pot, fitting lid and cooking utensil may meet a household need that none meets alone. This changes what recipients can obtain, rather than merely rearranging the display. Donor take-back remains the safeguard for leftovers; kit building is the proposed source of additional reuse.

Run a short staffed session on each of four Saturdays. One volunteer checks clean, usable, small household items and retains their numbered tags; the other helps residents assemble kits around an explicit use, such as a basic cooking set or desk stationery set. Exclude hazardous electronics, unsafe objects and anything requiring heavy lifting. Collect neither names nor money.

Donors remain present and retain responsibility for their contributions. Place a proposed kit on the table only with every contributing donor’s agreement. Record its component numbers on a tag. A recipient must inspect and want the components; nobody must accept unwanted extras to obtain one useful object. Allow individual transfers when a kit attracts no interest. Pause admissions when the table fills or supervision becomes difficult.

Close intake before the session ends. Donors reclaim every unclaimed component, including incomplete kits. Offer the municipal disposal guide without implying that it guarantees collection. Leave no inventory between Saturdays. Confirm a public-site abandonment procedure before launch, since deliberate dumping remains possible.

Record components reused, kits transferred, unclaimed components, abandoned objects and cleanup minutes. Separately count handling-related refusals and occasions when someone wants a kit but cannot carry it. Offer lighter subsets and reachable inspection without promising transport.

This needs only the table, tags, guide and two volunteers. It assumes complementary donations arrive together and volunteers can judge basic compatibility. Bundling may increase carrying exclusion or waste time when arrivals are sparse.
EXPAND.experiment: On Saturday one, use alternating short periods of individual-item offers and kit assembly, retaining the same intake and take-back rules throughout. Record components transferred per period, volunteer assembly effort, leftovers, cleanup minutes and carrying-related failures. Ask kit recipients anonymously whether they wanted every component. The mechanism is weakened if kits do not improve component reuse, routinely contain unwanted extras, or increase carrying exclusion. Differences in arrivals make this a feasibility check, not a causal estimate.

EXPAND.title: Demonstrate before accepting: an inspectable exchange
EXPAND.proposal:
The main mechanism is reducing uncertainty about whether an unfamiliar used item actually works. Donors demonstrate an item's ordinary use, and recipients inspect it before accepting. This could turn offers rejected through distrust into reuse while screening out objects that would merely transfer a disposal problem. Donor take-back supplies the leftover safeguard; demonstration is the proposed additional source of useful exchanges.

Run a short staffed session on each of four Saturdays. Accept only clean, small household items whose relevant function can be checked safely at the table without power, water, tools or consumable supplies: for example, checking a storage box's lid, a manual mechanism or a bag's fastening. Exclude hazardous electronics, sharp or unsafe objects, and items requiring heavy lifting. Collect neither names nor money.

One volunteer manages admissions and supervision; the other supports inspection and records outcomes. Each printed tag identifies the item and records what was demonstrated and any disclosed defect. Mark untested properties explicitly. A demonstration is evidence of a limited function, not a safety certification. Donors stay with their goods until a recipient accepts them and removes them. Pause admissions whenever supervision or table space becomes inadequate.

Close intake before closing time. Donors take all unclaimed items away. Offer the municipal disposal guide for rejected or unwanted goods. Inspect the surrounding area and record any abandonment. Before launch, verify an existing authorized response for abandoned objects; the guide alone does not establish one, and volunteers have no storage option.

Count admitted items, completed transfers, leftovers returned, abandoned objects and cleanup minutes. Separately tally handling-related refusals and wanted transfers prevented by lifting or carrying difficulties. Place inspection items within easy reach and allow inspection without lifting. This approach assumes demonstrations are informative and attendance is modest; it excludes useful goods that cannot be checked with the available resources.
EXPAND.experiment: During the first Saturday, alternate comparable eligible offers between ordinary description-and-inspection and an explicit donor demonstration; retain identical admission and take-back rules. Use tags to count offers, transfers, defects discovered and handling failures in each group, plus overall leftovers and cleanup minutes. Ask recipients one optional anonymous question: did the demonstration change their willingness to accept? If demonstrations repeatedly add delay without changing acceptance or uncovering defects, drop the extra step. Small numbers and differences between items will limit conclusions.
